newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Concern over future undercuts Hebron joy.
newsitem.headline: Concern over future undercuts Hebron joy.

text.p: Concern for the future haunted Palestinians in Hebron at dawn on Friday even as they celebrated the end of Israel's 30-year occupation in most of the West Bank town.
Israeli soldiers pulled out of the military headquarters and Palestinian police rolled in to take charge of self-rule in 80 percent of the town, a traditional flashpoint of Arab-Israeli violence.
"I am so happy to see them leave. This will give a chance for peace," said Ziad Abu Rajab, an employee of the Hebron municipality, as Israeli army vehicles left the hilltop headquarters.
"But my joy is incomplete. They will still be in the downtown area," he said.
Only a small crowd was on hand to witness the handshake between officers from the two sides that set the long-delayed Israeli redeployment in motion.
A lone Palestinian climbed a tall antenna atop the headquarters to raise the Palestinian flag over the building which President Yasser Arafat was expected to visit within a few days.
It took several minutes for the young Palestinian to reach the top. When he got there, he pulled the flag out of the back of his trousers and attached it to the antenna.
The mood was subdued. Palestinians who waited in the rain and cold until midnight for the expected handover went home in disappointment after being told it would take place only on Friday morning.
Few had returned by 6 a.m. when the ceremony took place.

Israeli soldiers who abandoned the headquarters moved into the Hebron town centre to patrol 20 percent of Hebron, where about 400 Jewish settlers rub shoulders with more than 20,000 Palestinians who remain under Israeli occupation.
A fear of violence hovered over the city holy to Moslem and Jew as the burial place of the biblical Abraham.
Jewish settlers charged that the Israeli army pullout endangered their presence in the town. Palestinians feared settlers would resort to violence.

Israeli soldiers spent most of Thursday removing hardware from military bases across the city. Outside the headquarters, Palestinians gathered in the cold to cheer as trucks ferried out watchtowers and concrete blocks.
Soldiers uprooted a palm sibling and loaded it on a truck leaving the headquarters.
"Take everything and go. Just go. We don't want to see your faces here," shouted one young Palestinian as the trucks left.
"I am going to miss you," another Palestinian shouted sarcastically at an Israeli soldier peering from the back of a military jeep as it sped down a narrow winding road out of the grey building.
Supporters of Palestinian President Arafat danced with pictures of their leader.
Before the handover, Palestinian Preventive Security Chief Jibril Rajoub inspected the building where once suspected Palestinian militants were held prisoner.
"I am happy to enter, not as a prisoner, but as a policeman which is liberating this valuable part of the homeland," he told reporters.
